method: microspectrophotometry of single photoreceptor cells, glass eels

method: frozen eyeball homogenised in 1% CHAPS buffer under dim red light (>640 nm), extract centrifuged at 50,000 g, extraction repeated until the supernatant was colourless (four extracts); absorption spectra at 28 C, hydroxylamine added to 100 mM, residual pigment bleached with orange and yellow light; absorption maximum read from the resulting difference spectrum
conditions: deep-sea snailfish taken at the Hatoma Knoll hydrothermal vent field, Okinawa Trough, 1480-1530 m, by ROV; number of fish and collection date not stated, the spectroscopy describing one frozen eyeball, the other eye kept for RNA, which implies a single fish; one eyeball kept for RNA and the other frozen for protein; the absolute spectrum also showed a component near 410 nm (a hydroxylamine-labile difference peak at 414 nm the authors could not identify) alongside the 480 nm absorption they attribute to rhodopsin; the recombinant protein expressed in HEK293EBNA cells with 11-cis retinal also peaked at 480 nm; no replicate count or statistics given for the spectra; the abstract's link to blue-light sensitivity is the authors' inference, not measured

units: nm (peak of the ERG spectral sensitivity curve)
eye: whole-eye ERG, dark-adapted (scotopic, most likely rod-mediated per the authors)
method: electroretinography (b-wave), dark-adapted whole-eye ERG; sensitivity from irradiance needed for a 5 microvolt criterion response
conditions: wild fish taken by daytime bottom trawl at 100-117 m in the Apostle Islands region of Lake Superior on 13 Nov 2012 and 26 June 2013 and held at the University of Minnesota Duluth (kiyi tested within 4 days of capture, siscowet within 3 weeks, sculpin within 2 months); number of fish per species and body sizes not stated; held in refrigerated dark rooms lit indirectly by dim red light at 3-6 C, dark-adapted 30 min before testing; the authors state the data are limited to scotopic visual sensitivity most likely mediated by the rod photoreceptors, and no light-adapted (photopic or cone) response was tested; anaesthetised with buffered 0.002% MS-222 and immobilised with pancuronium bromide; ERG with a silver-silver chloride electrode in the vitreous, monochromatic light 400-700 nm in 25 nm steps in random order from a 100 W tungsten-halogen lamp, b-wave criterion of 5 microvolts set at 400 nm and met at other wavelengths with neutral-density filters; the deepwater sculpin needed at least 190 s between flashes to avoid transient bleaching; the peak is resolved only to the 25 nm stimulus step; curves are group means with SE bars and no statistical test between species is reported; all three species peaked at 525 nm with broad sensitivity 500-550 nm, the deepwater sculpin broader (475-550 nm); the abstract's full-moon depth for the sculpin (45 m) differs from the Results' figure (63 m per the page text read), a separate depth-profile result not logged here; the Discussion says fish were trawled during both day and night, against the Methods' daytime trawls

value: physiological hearing threshold tuned to 5 kHz in both sexes
method: extracellular suction-electrode recordings from axons of auditory interneurons in the neck connective, pure sine tones 3-50 kHz; male threshold curve recorded in this study (N = 4) and compared with a female threshold curve adapted from earlier work (Lakes-Harlan, Stölting and Stumpner 1999, Proc R Soc B 266: 1161-1167, the paper's ref. 17)
conditions: flies emerged from pupae taken from infected cicadas (Okanagana rimosa) collected in Michigan, USA, pupae held at 4 C for up to six months, males also swept from vegetation; electrophysiology N = 4 males in this study; the female curve (N = 3, Fig 2 caption) is adapted from the 1999 paper, not newly recorded, so the female half of 'both sexes' is carried from earlier data; no threshold in dB SPL at 5 kHz is printed; threshold curves of the sexes very similar in tuning and sensitivity, males relatively insensitive in the ultrasonic range; no statistical test for the threshold comparison was read; separate behavioural phonotaxis tests on 17 males (each up to three times) found males oriented to the host song but often incompletely, and scored significantly higher for 9 kHz than 5 kHz song models (p = 0.0113, t = 3.27, df = 11, paired t-test) even though 5 kHz is the best hearing frequency; the male ear is about 8% narrower than the female ear
